precepts.text: How doth the city sit solitary, that was full of people! how is she become as a widow! she that was great among the nations, and princess among the provinces, how is she become tributary! So we are the widow. Christ is making reference back to that in Luke 18.
precepts.point: Nevertheless when the Son of man cometh, shall he find faith on the earth? Will there be faith? Will brothers and sisters still be doing that? That is the question. Will you believe to pray for vengeance? Will you believe that thing? That is what Christ is asking.

note.label: The Waters of Noah Will Be Fire

precepts.why:
In the parable “there was a widow in that city; and she came unto him, saying, Avenge me of mine adversary.” We are that widow. The Lord said he was married unto us, but because we sinned, he refused us. Jeremiah shows the same widow: “How doth the city sit solitary, that was full of people! how is she become as a widow!”

“she that was great among the nations, and princess among the provinces, how is she become tributary”! That is Israel: once full of people, great among the nations, a princess among the provinces, now alone, cast off like a widow, and paying tribute to others. Christ is making reference back to that in Luke 18.

So the widow crying “Avenge me of mine adversary” is us, the twelve tribes, crying for vengeance on our enemies. We want revenge. “he would not for a while”, just as the Lord kept silence for a time, but “because this widow troubleth me, I will avenge her, lest by her continual coming she weary me.” Because the twelve tribes trouble him, he will avenge her. That is the key: pray for vengeance and don't stop.

“And shall not God avenge his own elect, which cry day and night unto him”? We are the elect, crying day and night, three times a day. Some of our people call it unjust that God put us in slavery and punished us, and ask why an all-loving God would do that. It is not unjust: you punish your kids when they go off, and likewise the Lord. “I tell you that he will avenge them speedily.” The question Christ asks is whether, when he comes, he will find that faith: will the widow still be praying for vengeance?

precepts.text: Jerusalem sinned and her nakedness was seen; nakedness is sin.
precepts.point: Remember this is an illustrated story. The fig leaves and aprons represent them trying to cover their transgressions.

note.label: Genesis 3: The Craftiness of Your Enemy

precepts.why:
“Jerusalem hath grievously sinned; therefore she is removed: all that honoured her despise her, because they have seen her nakedness”. Jerusalem sinned, and what was seen was her nakedness. Nakedness is sin.

So when “the eyes of them both were opened, and they knew that they were naked”, they were not literally naked. They knew they were in sin, and the fig leaf aprons were their attempt to cover the transgression.

precepts.text: Mine eyes run down with water, because the comforter that should relieve my soul is far from me.
precepts.point: They which make oil within their walls and tread their winepresses still suffer thirst. This is the curse where you plant vineyards and do not eat from them, left neither corn nor wine.

note.label: Job 24: The Crimes of the Oppressor

precepts.why:
Our children given to another people brings this weeping: “For these things I weep; mine eye, mine eye runneth down with water, because the comforter that should relieve my soul is far from me: my children are desolate, because the enemy prevailed.”

The children are desolate because the enemy prevailed, plucked from the breast as Job says, and the comforter that should relieve the soul is far away. Those who make oil within their walls and tread their winepresses still suffer thirst: that is the curse where you plant vineyards and do not eat from them, left neither corn nor wine.

precepts.text: All thy lovers have forgotten thee and seek thee not, for the Most High wounded thee with the wound of an enemy for the multitude of thine iniquity.
precepts.point: Israel's lovers and friends were other nations serving other gods, and when it got real they turned their backs, just as the Most High warned.

note.label: Lamentations 1: The City That Sits Solitary

precepts.why:
Jerusalem weeps and “among all her lovers she hath none to comfort her: all her friends have dealt treacherously with her, they are become her enemies.” Jeremiah had already said it: “All thy lovers have forgotten thee; they seek thee not; for I have wounded thee with the wound of an enemy, with the chastisement of a cruel one, for the multitude of thine iniquity; because thy sins were increased.”

Israel's lovers and friends were other nations serving other gods, and when it got real they turned their backs, just as the Most High warned. And it was he who wounded her, “with the wound of an enemy”, for the multitude of her iniquity. That is how the city that was full of people, great among the nations and princess among the provinces, came to sit solitary as a widow, with no one to comfort her.

precepts.text: The heathen came into the Most High's inheritance, defiled His holy temple, and laid Jerusalem on heaps.
precepts.point: All her people sigh and seek bread, and they gave their pleasant things for meat to relieve the soul; when things get that serious, people give up whatever they once thought they could not live without.

note.label: Lamentations 1: The City That Sits Solitary

precepts.why:
Jerusalem “hath seen that the heathen entered into her sanctuary, whom thou didst command that they should not enter into thy congregation.” The psalm mourns the same thing: “O God, the heathen are come into thine inheritance; thy holy temple have they defiled; they have laid Jerusalem on heaps.”

The heathen came into the Most High's inheritance, defiled His holy temple, and laid Jerusalem on heaps. That is why she is removed, why “all that honoured her despise her”, and why she has no comforter: she grievously sinned, and the ones the Most High commanded should not enter His congregation walked into her sanctuary.

precepts.text: On the side of the oppressor there was power, but the oppressed had no comforter, which came to pass in the Babylonian captivity.
precepts.point: She weeps because the comforter that should relieve her soul is far from her; there was oppression but no comforter to relieve them.

note.label: Lamentations 1: The City That Sits Solitary

precepts.why:
Jerusalem weeps “because the comforter that should relieve my soul is far from me.” Solomon saw that condition: “So I returned, and considered all the oppressions that are done under the sun: and behold the tears of such as were oppressed, and they had no comforter; and on the side of their oppressors there was power; but they had no comforter.”

On the side of the oppressor there was power, but the oppressed had no comforter. That came to pass in the Babylonian captivity: the Most High trod under foot all her mighty men, called an assembly to crush her young men, the leaders taken out first, and delivered her into the hands of those from whom she could not rise up. There was oppression, but no comforter to relieve them.

precepts.text: Those who afflicted and rejoiced over Israel will be grieved for their own desolation, and fire shall come upon Babylon the great.
precepts.point: Even in judgment our forefathers still prayed for the destruction of the enemy, asking the Most High to render to them all their wickedness and do to them as He had done to Jerusalem.

note.label: Lamentations 1: The City That Sits Solitary

precepts.why:
Even in judgment our forefathers still prayed for the destruction of the enemy: “Let all their wickedness come before thee; and do unto them, as thou hast done unto me for all my transgressions.” Baruch gives the answer to that prayer. “Miserable are they that afflicted thee, and rejoiced at thy fall. Miserable are the cities which thy children served: miserable is she that received thy sons.”

Her enemies “are glad that thou hast done it”; but “as she rejoiced at thy ruin, and was glad of thy fall: so shall she be grieved for her own desolation. For I will take away the rejoicing of her great multitude, and her pride shall be turned into mourning.”

“For fire shall come upon her from the Everlasting, long to endure; and she shall be inhabited of devils for a great time.” Those who afflicted and rejoiced over Israel will be grieved for their own desolation, and fire shall come upon Babylon the great. The day the Most High has called will come, and “they shall be like unto me.”
